title: Exponential worst-case hardness implies mild average-case hardness in NP
formal:
Is the implication \(H_{\mathrm{worst}}\Rightarrow H_{\mathrm{mild}}\) true, where
\[
H_{\mathrm{worst}}:\quad\exists L\in\mathrm{NP}\ \exists\alpha\in\mathbb Q\cap(0,1)\ \exists N\ge1\ \forall n\ge N\ \forall C\in\mathcal C(n,\lfloor2^{\alpha n}\rfloor)\ \exists x\in\{0,1\}^n:\ C(x)\ne1_L(x),
\]
and
\[
H_{\mathrm{mild}}:\quad\exists M\in\mathrm{NP}\ \exists\beta\in\mathbb Q\cap(0,1)\ \exists a,N'\in\mathbb Z_{\ge1}\ \forall n\ge N'\ \forall C\in\mathcal C(n,\lfloor2^{\beta n}\rfloor):\quad
\Pr_{x\sim U_n}[C(x)\ne1_M(x)]\ge n^{-a}?
\]
Here \(\mathcal C(n,s)\) is the class of deterministic Boolean circuits with \(n\) input bits and at most \(s\) gates, and \(U_n\) is the uniform distribution on those bits. No additional cryptographic, average-case or nondeterministic hardness assumption is permitted.
why: A hard exceptional input does not explain why a uniformly sampled instance should be hard. The question asks whether exponential worst-case difficulty within NP necessarily supplies a language with a substantial density of hard inputs at the same exponential scale.

importance.reason: This is a quantitative form of the central gap between worst-case NP hardness and useful average-case prediction hardness. Preserving exponential circuit hardness would connect strong lower-bound assumptions to pseudorandomness without importing a separate cryptographic hypothesis.

sentences: The premise is an NP language that requires exponentially large Boolean circuits in the worst case.
The conclusion asks for another NP language on which exponentially large circuits err on an inverse-polynomial fraction of uniformly random inputs.
Both hardness guarantees must hold at every sufficiently large input length.
The proposed implication permits any proof method and adds no cryptographic assumption.
It isolates the quantitative worst-to-average gap from both polynomial-time average complexity and amplification of already established average hardness.

definitions:
A language is a subset of all finite binary strings, and \(1_L\) is its membership bit. Membership in \(\mathrm{NP}\) means there is one deterministic Turing-machine verifier \(V\) and one polynomial \(p\) such that, for every string \(x\), membership is equivalent to the existence of a certificate \(y\) of length at most \(p(|x|)\) for which \(V(x,y)=1\). The verifier halts in time polynomial in the lengths of its two inputs. It receives neither advice depending on the input length nor an oracle. The two languages in the implication may use different verifiers and polynomials.

A circuit is a finite acyclic directed graph with labeled input vertices \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\), constants zero and one available, AND and OR gates of fan-in two, NOT gates of fan-in one, and one designated output. Fan-out is unrestricted. Size counts Boolean operation gates; input vertices and the two available constants are not charged. Direct output of an input or constant is allowed. There is no requirement that circuits for different lengths, or different approximations at one length, be produced uniformly by an algorithm. No nondeterministic, oracle or unbounded-fan-in gates are allowed.

The probability in \(H_{\mathrm{mild}}\) is exactly the number of erroneous inputs divided by \(2^n\). Circuits are deterministic, so no internal-coin probability enters this definition. The uniform distribution is fixed; a construction may not replace it by an unspecified samplable distribution. No balance condition is imposed on the accepted fraction of either language. In particular, the conclusion is mild prediction hardness, not near-half error or one-wayness.

Both hypotheses assert their respective lower bound at every sufficiently large length. Their thresholds are fixed independently of circuits and lengths. The constants and the language in the conclusion may depend on witnesses to the premise, but once chosen they must work for all sufficiently large lengths. Neither a bound only at infinitely many lengths nor a loss from \(2^{\Omega(n)}\) to \(2^{n^{\gamma}}\) with \(\gamma<1\) gives the stated conclusion. The exponent constants \(\alpha,\beta\) need not coincide, and the polynomial-error exponent \(a\) is not prescribed.

This is an existence implication between two quantitatively specified hardness assertions. It does not demand a black-box oracle reduction, a many-one map from each input of \(L\), an algorithm taking a verifier as input, or a prescribed syntactic relation between the two languages. Any valid proof of the implication is admissible. Conversely, ruling out a particular class of reductions does not refute the implication. Its full negation is \(H_{\mathrm{worst}}\land\neg H_{\mathrm{mild}}\); it includes establishing the premise, rather than merely assuming the conclusion false.

The all-length nonuniform exponential premise is stronger and different from \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\). The selected target therefore does not duplicate the separate uniform, average-running-time implication recorded in TCS-0012. It also differs from TCS-6703, which starts with an already mildly hard balanced language and asks to strengthen the error bound.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the implication or its full logical negation under the definitions above. A positive answer may assume the displayed worst-case hypothesis without proving it, but cannot add another unproved hypothesis. A negative answer must prove that hypothesis together with failure of every possible mild-hardness witness. A relativized counterexample or black-box reduction barrier alone is insufficient.

source_formulation.text: Section 7.5 asks for an NP counterpart of worst-case-to-average-case amplification preserving hardness up to a fixed power and input length up to a constant factor. This card selects the high-end existential implication with inverse-polynomial error and all sufficiently large lengths. It is an announced editorial default and a precise subgoal of the broader reduction program, not a verbatim theorem conjectured with these quantifiers. context_blocks.text: For larger complexity classes, truth-table encoding and local decoding can spread worst-case hardness across many inputs. Keeping the resulting membership language inside NP is the obstacle highlighted by the source.

Hirahara obtains non-black-box reductions for specific metacomputational approximation problems. The checked statements require specific hardness or completeness conditions; they do not deduce the displayed exponential uniform-distribution conclusion from its sole premise.

The 2025 work explicitly discusses the remaining gap between exponential worst-case hardness and average-case hardness of NP. Its positive cryptographic constructions add obfuscation and other specified assumptions, which this target does not allow.
